title: Intro to Computer Memory: Linked Lists
summary: Explains contiguous memory (arrays and Python lists, fast index lookups) versus dynamic memory (pieces anywhere, linked by pointers). A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. The lesson builds Node and LinkedList classes with add, iterate and remove methods. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Build a singly linked list in Python and explain when it beats a regular list.

steps.title: Read the lesson
steps.detail: Read the Computer Memory and Linked Lists page. The assigned readings (How Computer Memory Works, and pages 44–47 of 'Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective') go deeper if you have time.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain contiguous vs dynamic memory with one tradeoff each.

steps.title: Run the curriculum's linked list
steps.detail: Save and run this. Note: the lesson's usage example calls ll.addNode, but the method is named add_node, so use add_node.

steps.title: Add remove_node and draw it
steps.detail: Copy the lesson's remove_node method in, remove 3, and sketch boxes and arrows on paper showing which pointer changed.
steps.doneWhen: iterate() prints 0, 2, 4 and your sketch shows 2 now pointing to 4.

steps.title: Talk through Reverse a Linked List
steps.detail: Reverse a Linked List is one of the assignments and a very common interview question. Before coding, say the plan (walk the list with prev, current and next, flipping each arrow) and its Big-O: time O(n), space O(1).
steps.doneWhen: You can explain the three-pointer approach out loud.
